case_study_insert.main_stem: Vela Vintage Fashion (VVF) is a private limited company in the second-hand fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 25. Founded in 2018 by Priya Vela, the business reconditions and sells vintage clothing through its e-commerce website and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. VVF plans to invest $240,000 in a new photography studio and packing area, financed by $150,000 hire purchase and $90,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $126,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $28.00, and currently produces 18,000 units a year. VVF faces two problems: damage in transit has reached 3.4% and return requests in its online orders are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: E-commerce Operations Report — Q1 2026: VVF listed 3,400 new vintage items and dispatched 18,000 units over the year, with a damage-in-transit rate of 3.4%, up from 2.0% a year earlier. Return requests rose to 12.6% of orders. Customer complaints increased from 16 to 29 a month. Average dispatch time is 3.8 days. A survey of 600 vintage-fashion shoppers found 74% worry about item condition and 63% trust detailed photographs. A skills check shows 7 of 25 staff need training on the new packing process; external workshops cost $560 each.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Vela Vintage Fashion as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate agreements. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.80 to $14.56 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Second-hand garment collection and cleaning input costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, while online resale consumer spending grew 6.4%.

questions.question_text: VVF is financing part of its $240,000 expansion through $150,000 of hire purchase. Explain two advantages for VVF of using hire purchase rather than a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $150,000 cost of the photography studio and packing equipment into regular instalments, so VVF does not need the full sum upfront and can keep the $90,000 retained profit as working capital. That preserves cash against fixed costs of $126,000 a year while the business deals with 3.4% damage in transit and 12.6% return requests.

Point 2: The asset is used immediately while it is being paid for, so the studio can start producing the detailed photographs that 63% of surveyed vintage shoppers trust, supporting sales of 18,000 units. Unlike a bank loan, hire purchase does not require a separate lump-sum deposit or the same level of collateral negotiation, which suits a small 25-staff firm whose founder Priya Vela wants to keep control.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to VVF's hire purchase, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: VVF is promoting a new curated vintage collection. Consider print advertising in a lifestyle magazine, sponsorship of a fashion event, or social-media influencer marketing. Which should VVF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Lifestyle magazine print advertising: Print can showcase high-quality photographs of the vintage collection and reach readers interested in style, giving a credible, tangible impression. However, magazines have long lead times, high upfront costs and no direct link to the e-commerce website, so conversion cannot be measured. For a 25-staff firm funding a $240,000 studio with $126,000 fixed costs, untrackable print spend is hard to justify.

Fashion event sponsorship: Sponsoring a vintage or fashion fair puts the brand in front of engaged buyers and creates content for the website. It also builds personal credibility for Priya Vela's brand. The drawbacks are significant cost and a short-lived, location-specific impact; the audience may be small, and there is no guarantee that attendees become online buyers, which limits the contribution to 18,000 units of annual sales.

Social-media influencer marketing: The insert shows 74% of vintage shoppers worry about item condition and 63% trust detailed photographs. Influencers can demonstrate condition and styling honestly, link directly to the e-commerce site, and provide measurable engagement at low cost. They reach a national audience that a local event cannot, though results depend on choosing credible, style-matched partners and may build more slowly than a one-off event.

Recommendation: VVF should choose social-media influencer marketing. It addresses the exact concerns in the survey, drives measurable traffic to the website and scales nationally at a fraction of print or event costs. Magazine advertising is rejected as slow and unmeasurable, and fashion-event sponsorship is rejected as expensive and geographically limited for an online business with $126,000 fixed costs. VVF should pair influencers with the new studio photographs rather than either rejected option.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to VVF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to VVF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to VVF with a justified recommendation explaining why print and event sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: VVF has a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership and faces 3.4% damage in transit. Explain two benefits for VVF of this leadership style with its experienced reconditioning staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership lets experienced reconditioning staff make their own decisions about how to clean and pack delicate vintage items, using their specialist judgement to reduce the 3.4% damage-in-transit rate. Faster local decisions also help cut the 3.8-day dispatch time without waiting for approval through layers, which suits a flat structure of 25 employees.

Point 2: Delegation raises motivation and ownership among skilled workers, which can help stabilise the rising 12.6% return requests because staff who take pride in condition are less likely to misdescribe items. Higher engagement supports output of 18,000 units and makes better use of the $240,000 photography studio and packing area without adding supervisory costs.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to VVF's damage rate, returns and staffing.

questions.question_text: VVF wants to reduce the 3.4% damage in transit. Consider a bonus paid per order packed correctly or profit sharing for all staff. Which should VVF introduce? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Bonus per order packed correctly: A targeted bonus rewards the specific behaviour that lowers the 3.4% damage rate, giving packers an immediate financial incentive to check padding and labels. It is cheap to operate because it is variable cost, paid only when performance improves, and fits 25 staff who can see a direct link between care and reward. Weaknesses are that it may encourage rushing on unmeasured tasks, and it can create rivalry that harms team work in the packing area.

Profit sharing for all staff: Sharing a share of profits builds loyalty across the whole business and aligns everyone with customer satisfaction, which could reduce both 3.4% damage and 12.6% return requests. It suits a flat, laissez-faire culture and retains staff. However, the link to an individual packer's actions is weak, payouts depend on overall profit that is affected by $126,000 fixed costs and 8.9% input inflation, and the reward may feel too distant to change daily behaviour quickly.

Decision: VVF should introduce the bonus per order packed correctly, with profit sharing considered later. The bonus attacks the stated 3.4% damage problem directly, is affordable because it is paid from improved output of 18,000 units, and gives fast feedback; profit sharing is rejected for now because its rewards are too diffuse and uncertain against current input-cost pressure, though it could support retention once damage is under control.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivators with limited application to VVF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both motivators applied to VVF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both motivators applied to VVF with a justified decision covering cost, targeting and the damage-rate problem.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VVF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $126,000 ÷ ($28.00 − $14.00) = $126,000 ÷ $14.00 = 9,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 9,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $28.00 − $14.00 = $14.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $14.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VVF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 9,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 18,000 units shows a margin of safety of 9,000 units, indicating the fall in sales the business could absorb before the $240,000 studio and packing area stop covering costs.
2. Contribution per unit of $14.00 lets managers model a price rise: a $2 increase to $30.00 would give $16.00 contribution, so they can assess whether the 63% of shoppers who trust detailed photographs would accept a higher price for better-listed items.
3. Fixed costs and contribution help assess whether the $150,000 hire-purchase instalments can be met from the contribution on 18,000 units before more equipment is financed.
4. Unit cost data ($126,000 ÷ 18,000 units + $14.00 = $21.00 a unit) allows monthly benchmarking, so managers can monitor the 3.4% damage-in-transit rate and 12.6% return requests as avoidable costs.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 9,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $14.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 9,000 units versus 18,000-unit output; testing a $2 price rise against $14.00 contribution; hire-purchase affordability of $150,000; and unit-cost benchmarking at $21.00 to monitor 3.4% damage and 12.6% returns.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VVF's liquidity position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has VVF's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $48,000 inventories + $22,000 trade receivables + $14,000 cash = $84,000; 2025 current assets = $40,000 + $30,000 + $20,000 = $90,000. The 2024 liquidity comparison is $84,000 ÷ $60,000 = 1.40; for 2025 it is $90,000 ÷ $50,000 = 1.80. The stricter 2024 measure is ($84,000 − $48,000) ÷ $60,000 = $36,000 ÷ $60,000 = 0.60; for 2025 it is ($90,000 − $40,000) ÷ $50,000 = $50,000 ÷ $50,000 = 1.00.

Evaluation: Short-term solvency has improved. The broader measure rose from 1.40 to 1.80 because current liabilities fell from $60,000 to $50,000 while current assets rose from $84,000 to $90,000. The stricter measure improved from 0.60 to 1.00, so VVF can now meet short-term obligations without depending on inventory — useful when vintage stock can be slow to sell and 3.4% of items are damaged in transit. The more convincing signal is the stricter measure, because its improvement is not reliant on stock that may be harder to sell. However, trade receivables rose from $22,000 to $30,000, tying up cash, and the stricter measure only just reaches 1.00, leaving a thin cushion if online payment platforms delay settlement as the $240,000 expansion begins.

Conclusion: VVF's liquidity has improved, but the margin is modest. Both the broader measure (1.40 to 1.80) and the stricter measure (0.60 to 1.00) moved favourably, yet the latter leaves little headroom. Management should monitor the rising receivables and keep cash control tight before committing further to the studio expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liability movements and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VVF of selling directly to customers through its own e-commerce website.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Its own e-commerce website lets VVF show the detailed photographs that 63% of surveyed vintage shoppers trust, directly tackling the 74% who worry about item condition and helping reduce the 12.6% return rate. Direct sales also avoid intermediary margins, protecting the $28.00 selling price and the $14.00 contribution needed to justify the $240,000 studio investment and 18,000-unit output.

Disadvantage: Running a website adds fixed costs and requires constant updates, packaging and dispatch, which already show 3.4% damage in transit and 3.8-day dispatch times. Without a physical shop, customers cannot inspect vintage items in person, so condition disputes may rise, and the 25-staff team needs training on the new packing process at $560 per workshop to keep service reliable.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VVF's survey data, damage rate and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 8.9% rise in garment input costs will affect VVF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): The insert does not state whether VVF's $150,000 hire-purchase agreement carries a variable rate, so only a labelled illustration is defensible: if it did, a 0.75-point rise would add about $1,125 a year (0.0075 × $150,000). That is small against $126,000 fixed costs, and if the agreement is fixed the direct effect is zero. Dearer credit could still slow the 6.4% growth in online resale spending, but VVF can largely manage this risk.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $14.56 per hour): The insert gives 25 staff but no hours or pay rates, so no annual wage total can be invented. The honest test is productivity — 18,000 units ÷ 25 staff = 720 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if the 3.4% damage rate and 12.6% return requests absorb staff time, unit labour cost rises and the $14.00 contribution per unit shrinks. Training 7 staff at $560 each on the new packing process would protect productivity.

Garment input-cost inflation (8.9%): The insert never decomposes the $14.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be computed: if the whole variable cost rose 8.9%, that adds 8.9% × $14.00 = about $1.25 a unit; at 18,000 units this is roughly $22,500 a year (18,000 × $1.25). Even a partial rise cuts contribution on every unit, and damaged items waste the input altogether. The 63% of shoppers who trust detailed photographs may support a modest price rise, but the pressure is continuous.

Conclusion: The 8.9% rise in garment input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 18,000 units and directly erodes the $14.00 contribution that supports the $240,000 expansion, whereas the interest effect is at most about $1,125 a year and uncertain, and the wage impact can be offset if 720-unit productivity is maintained through training and better packing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to VVF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VVF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to VVF with a well-justified judgement that garment input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
